output.query: GBM recurrence management NCSE tumor-related epilepsy treatment

results.finding: Levetiracetam is commonly used as first-line antiseizure medication in GBM-related epilepsy; lacosamide and valproate have also been evaluated in this population.
Non-convulsive status epilepticus in patients with glioblastoma is underdiagnosed; EEG is required for detection, as clinical examination alone is insufficient.
Elevated rCBV on perfusion MRI has been reported to discriminate tumor recurrence from radiation necrosis with approximately 87% sensitivity.
Corticosteroid dose reduction is associated with increased peritumoral edema and may correlate with increased seizure frequency in some glioblastoma series.
Bevacizumab, a VEGF inhibitor, has been associated with reduced seizure frequency in recurrent GBM, potentially through reduction of vascular permeability and peritumoral edema.

output.summary: Tumor-related epilepsy occurs in 30–50% of patients with glioblastoma; non-convulsive seizure activity is frequently underdiagnosed in this population and EEG monitoring is required for detection. Peritumoral edema from recurrent disease is a recognized precipitant of increased seizure frequency. High rCBV on perfusion MRI has been reported to distinguish tumor recurrence from radiation necrosis with sensitivity of approximately 87%. Antiseizure medications including levetiracetam and lacosamide are used in GBM-related epilepsy; valproate has also been studied in this context.

patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old White male retired electrician was brought to the emergency department by EMS after his wife called 911. She reported witnessing a brief generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds while he was sitting at the breakfast table. She noted he had been 'not himself' for the past three weeks — increasingly forgetful, having trouble with word-finding, and seeming confused in the mornings. After the witnessed seizure stopped, she expected him to recover within minutes as had occurred with prior episodes, but he remained minimally responsive and confused for over 25 minutes, prompting her call to 911. He has a known diagnosis of right temporal glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) diagnosed 8 months ago, status post gross total resection followed by concurrent temozolomide and radiation, now on maintenance temozolomide. He completed his most recent temozolomide cycle 11 days ago. He takes dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for peritumoral edema, which was recently tapered from 6 mg twice daily over the past two weeks per his neuro-oncologist's instruction. He has a known seizure disorder secondary to his brain tumor and takes levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. His wife reports he has been taking his levetiracetam consistently. He denies fever, headache, or new neurological symptoms when he can communicate.
